candidate.title: Matt Slick vs Aron Ra: Is Christianity True? (2014)
candidate.label: Christianity, evidence, and rational foundations
candidate.sourceNote: This assessment uses a complete timestamp-preserving paid transcript covering the full primary-speaker debate. Host Tim made two incidental Christian-aligned advocacy interventions; both complete host-led blocks and every directly dependent reply were frozen and excluded. Neither Matt Slick nor Aron Ra received credit or penalty for that material. All 43 selected moves had high-confidence attribution, so no further source-audio checks were required.
candidate.scoringNote: These AI-generated scores were computed once from a frozen 43-move ledger after two isolated primary judgments and anonymous adjudication of all 111 extracted disagreements, including both burden-completion judgments. The displayed 73–73 result is immutable; publication prose and rhetorical-tag review cannot change it.

finalArgument.thesis: Christianity better accounts for rational knowledge when God is the necessary, noncontingent ground of logic, induction, and intelligibility.
premises: Scientific inquiry relies on logical validity and nature’s continuing regularity before any particular experiment can proceed.
Neither logic nor universal future uniformity can be established noncircularly by methods already presupposing them.
Abstract universal logical relations require an account beyond contingent matter and individual human minds.
The Christian God is noncontingent and transcendent, fitting the kind of ground those rational preconditions require.
Historical and theological objections must use accurate definitions, validated sources, and proportionate standards rather than asserted impossibility.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, Christianity supplies a coherent foundational explanation for rational practices used to assess every worldview, giving positive reason to regard it as true.

newArguments.title: Transcendental explanation
newArguments.text: If every inquiry necessarily relies on logic and induction, the central question is which worldview can explain that reliance. Christianity could gain force by deriving specific features of rational normativity from a necessarily rational God, then showing why naturalistic accounts cannot match those features without circularity or unexplained brute facts.

newArguments.title: Predictive divine grounding
newArguments.text: The foundational argument would become stronger if it identified risky expectations from divine rational governance, including stable discoverability, intersubjective logical convergence, or principled limits on disorder. Comparing those expectations with competing models would make the God hypothesis more than a label for regularity and answer the demand for explanatory content.

newArguments.title: Cumulative historical test
newArguments.text: The pro case could combine source proximity, independent attestation, hostile corroboration, explanatory scope, and comparable treatment of ancient figures. Christianity should receive support only if its central claims outperform natural and rival-religious explanations under the same threshold, avoiding selective standards while answering the demand for validated historical sources.

finalArgument.thesis: Christianity lacks adequate support because its theological additions lack independently testable evidence, public corroboration, and explanatory mechanisms.
premises: Responsible belief should track evidence, tested possibility, repeatability, and correction rather than protected conviction.
Observed regularities warrant provisional confidence without requiring certainty or relabeling that confidence as religious faith.
Reports that Christians believe doctrines establish belief facts but not the truth of Jesus, miracles, or God.
Truth-indicating consensus must extend beyond adherents and include investigators holding competing religious or nonreligious views.
Invoking God adds no explanatory content without a mechanism, distinctive prediction, or independently supported causal process.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, the debate provides inadequate public grounds for affirming Christianity as true, while evidential restraint remains better supported.

newArguments.title: Discriminating prediction test
newArguments.text: A theological hypothesis should specify observations more expected if Christianity is true than if naturalism or another religion is true. Public consistency, answered-prayer patterns, independently confirmed revelation, or unique historical evidence could be stated beforehand. Failure to produce discriminating expectations would support the contention that adding God does not improve the explanatory model.

newArguments.title: Cross-tradition comparison
newArguments.text: Competing religions generate sincere testimony, trained specialists, transformative experiences, and internally coherent interpretations. Identical criteria could measure Christian and non-Christian agreement, predictive success, correction mechanisms, and independent corroboration. If Christianity does not outperform alternatives, sectarian confidence would provide little public evidence for its exclusive truth.

newArguments.title: Mechanism and model selection
newArguments.text: Explanations can be compared by mechanisms, predictive precision, evidential fit, and added assumptions. The con case could formalize this comparison between a natural account and a God-added account, granting genuine predictive gain while penalizing unsupported complexity. That framework would turn the claim of superfluity into a transparent and defeasible inference.
